modules.title: Foundations: how creams, lotions and facial oils work
modules.overview: Learn the difference between water-free oils and water-based creams, what every ingredient in an emulsion does, and how to set up a clean, safe workspace before you heat a single drop. This module builds on simple butters and oils and takes you into proper emulsions.

lessons.title: Creams, lotions, facial oils and serums: what each one is
objectives: Explain what an emulsion is in plain words
Tell a lotion, a cream, a facial oil and a water-based serum apart
Identify whether a product is water-free (anhydrous) or water-based
Choose a sensible first product for your skills and budget

blocks.text: If you already make whipped shea butter or body oils, you are making **anhydrous** products. Anhydrous simply means "without water". Creams and lotions are different. They are mostly water, held together with oil in a smooth, white mixture. That mixture is called an **emulsion**, and making one well is the main skill of this course.

blocks.name: lotion-bottle
blocks.caption: A lotion in a pump bottle is usually an emulsion: water and oil held together by an emulsifier.

blocks.text: Oil and water do not mix on their own

Pour some groundnut oil into a cup of water and stir. Within a minute the oil floats back to the top. To keep tiny droplets of oil spread evenly through water, you need an **emulsifier**. An emulsifier is an ingredient with one end that likes water and one end that likes oil, so it sits between the two and stops the droplets joining back together. In home and small-scale skincare, the most common emulsifiers are sold as **emulsifying waxes**, white pellets or flakes that you melt with the oils.

Most body lotions and face creams are **oil-in-water** emulsions. That means small oil droplets float inside a larger amount of water. This is why a good lotion feels light, sinks in quickly and does not leave the heavy, greasy layer that pure shea butter can leave in hot weather.
The four product types in this course

head: Product
Water?
Typical feel
Needs a preservative?
rows: Yes, often about three quarters water
Yes, still mostly water but with more oil and thickener
Thicker, sits in a jar, richer

Yes, often aloe or hydrosol based

blocks.text: Notice the last column. The moment a product contains water, germs such as bacteria, yeast and mould can grow in it. A **broad-spectrum preservative**, one that works against all three, is not optional for creams, lotions or watery serums. Module 3 shows you how to choose one and use it correctly. Facial oils contain no water, so they do not need a preservative, but the oils can go rancid, which we deal with in Module 2.

blocks.title: Water-free versus water-based
items: Facial oil (anhydrous)
Cream or lotion (emulsion)
blocks.caption: Adding water changes the whole method: emulsifier, heat, preservative and testing all become necessary.

blocks.text: Why makers move from butters to creams

items: **Feel:** many customers in hot, humid cities like Lagos, Port Harcourt or Warri find a light lotion more comfortable than a solid butter.
**Spread:** a lotion spreads easily over large areas such as legs and arms, so a little goes a long way.
**Cost per jar:** water is cheap compared with shea butter or imported oils, but the savings are partly used up by the emulsifier, preservative, better packaging and testing.
**Face products:** facial skin often prefers lighter textures, so light creams and facial oils open a new range.

blocks.title: A cream is a step up in responsibility
blocks.text: A badly made butter usually just feels grainy. A badly made or unpreserved cream can grow germs that customers cannot see or smell and then rub onto their face. Treat every water-based product as a product that must be made cleanly, preserved properly and tested before anyone else uses it.

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing a first product
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kaduna sells whipped shea butter and has about ₦60,000 (approximate) to spend on learning. Customers keep asking for "something lighter for the face".
steps: She lists options: a body lotion, a face cream, a facial oil, or an aloe face gel.
She marks which contain water: lotion, face cream and aloe gel. Each needs an emulsifier or gelling agent, a broad-spectrum preservative and careful testing.
She compares equipment: a facial oil needs only a 0.01 g scale, clean glass dropper bottles and good oils. A lotion also needs a thermometer, stick blender, pH meter and preservative.
She decides to start selling a facial oil first, while practising a body lotion for her own use only until she has completed stability tests.
blocks.result: Halima gets a sellable, low-risk face product quickly and builds emulsion skills in parallel, without putting customers at risk while she learns.

blocks.text: Words you will meet again

items: **Water phase:** everything that dissolves in water, such as distilled water and glycerin.
**Oil phase:** oils, butters and the emulsifying wax.
**Cool-down phase:** heat-sensitive ingredients, including most preservatives, added after the cream has cooled.
**Batch formula:** the recipe written in percentages so it can be scaled to any size.
**Stability:** whether the product stays the same (no separation, smell or colour change) over time.

blocks.text: By the end of this course you will have made and tested one cream or lotion and one facial oil, written their formulas in percentages and grams, labelled them honestly and costed them. Take it one lesson at a time: the steps are simple when done in the right order.

takeaways: An emulsion is oil and water held together by an emulsifier.
Creams, lotions and watery serums contain water and always need a broad-spectrum preservative.
Facial oils are anhydrous: no preservative, but they need protection from rancidity.
Start selling the lowest-risk product while you practise emulsions for personal use.

lessons.title: Inside an emulsion: water phase, oil phase, emulsifier and cool-down
objectives: Name the job of each ingredient group in a cream
Read a published lotion formula and sort it into phases
Describe what an emulsifying wax is and how much is used
Explain why distilled water is used instead of tap water

blocks.text: Every cream, from a big brand to a home kitchen, is built from the same few building blocks. Once you can recognise them, any recipe becomes easy to read, and you can spot a recipe that is missing something important.

blocks.name: test-tube
blocks.caption: Each ingredient group in a cream has one clear job, just like each reagent in a laboratory test.

blocks.text: The water phase

This is the biggest part of a lotion. It usually contains **distilled water** plus a **humectant**, an ingredient that draws moisture to the skin. Vegetable glycerin is the most common humectant and is easy to find from cosmetic suppliers in Lagos, Abuja and online. Too much glycerin makes a cream sticky, so follow a tested recipe.

Use distilled water, not tap, borehole, sachet or bottled water. Making Skincare, a formulation teaching site, advises against tap, bottled or mineral water because the dissolved minerals and other content can shorten shelf life. Distilled or deionised water is sold by chemical shops and pharmacies, often for car batteries or laboratory use; buy a sealed bottle and check the label says distilled or deionised.
The oil phase

This holds your oils and butters and the emulsifying wax. Light oils such as sunflower, sweet almond or fractionated coconut oil give a thin, quick-absorbing feel. Butters such as shea or cocoa make a cream thicker and richer. In a lotion the oils are often around 10 to 25 percent of the total.
The emulsifying wax

Emulsifying wax (often shortened to e-wax) is a ready blend that does the emulsifying for you. Humblebee & Me, a respected formulation blog, describes three widely used ones: **Polawax**, **Emulsifying Wax NF**, and **Ritamulse SCG** (also sold as Emulsimulse). All three must be melted with the oils. Ordinary beeswax is **not** an emulsifier; it will not hold water and oil together for long, which is why beeswax and water recipes often separate.

How much? In Humblebee & Me's simple moisturising lotion, 3 percent Emulsifying Wax NF holds 10 percent oil. The same author writes that she usually uses 5 to 10 percent e-wax when the oils total about 25 percent. More oil needs more emulsifier. Always start from the supplier's recommended range for your exact wax.
The cool-down phase

Some ingredients are damaged by heat. The most important is the **preservative**. Many preservatives have a maximum temperature on their technical data sheet; for example, Humblebee & Me notes that Liquid Germall Plus tolerates heat only up to 50°C. So the preservative, and any essential oil or vitamin E, go in after the cream has cooled.

blocks.title: Building blocks of a basic lotion
items: Cool-down: preservative, extras
Emulsifying wax
Oils and butters
Humectant such as glycerin
Distilled water (largest part)
blocks.caption: Water forms the base, oils and emulsifier sit above it, and the tiny but essential cool-down phase goes in last.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a published lotion formula
blocks.context: For example, Amaka in Enugu finds Humblebee & Me's Super Simple Moisturizing Lotion and wants to understand it before trying it.
steps: She writes the ingredients with their percentages: distilled water 76.5%, vegetable glycerin 10%, Emulsifying Wax NF 3%, fractionated coconut oil 10%, Liquid Germall Plus 0.5%.
She adds them up: 76.5 + 10 + 3 + 10 + 0.5 = 100%. A proper formula always totals 100.
She sorts them: water phase = water and glycerin (86.5%); oil phase = e-wax and oil (13%); cool-down = preservative (0.5%).
She checks for the essentials: there is an emulsifier (e-wax) and a named broad-spectrum preservative. Nothing is missing.
blocks.result: Amaka can now read any lotion recipe, and she knows to reject one that has water but no emulsifier or no preservative.

blocks.text: Common optional extras

items: **Fatty thickeners** such as cetyl alcohol or cetearyl alcohol: these are waxy, not drying like rubbing alcohol, and they add body to a cream.
**Antioxidants** such as vitamin E (tocopherol): slow the oils going rancid. They do not stop germs.
**Plant extracts or hydrosols** such as rose water: these count as part of the water phase and still need preserving.
**Fragrance or essential oils:** optional, used at low levels in the cool-down phase, and best left out of face products for sensitive skin.

blocks.title: Same name, different product
blocks.text: "Emulsifying wax" sold in open bags in markets may not say which product it is. Buy from a supplier who can tell you the exact name and INCI (ingredient) name, such as Cetearyl Alcohol and Polysorbate 60 for Emulsifying Wax NF, and give you a usage rate. If the seller cannot tell you what it is, you cannot write an honest label.

A quick way to judge any recipe you find on WhatsApp, YouTube or Instagram is to ask three questions. Does it contain water or a watery ingredient such as aloe juice or rose water? If yes, does it name a real emulsifier, not just beeswax? And does it name a broad-spectrum preservative with a percentage? If any answer is no, the recipe is not ready for you to make for other people, however beautiful the video looks.
In the next lesson you set up a clean workspace. In Module 2 you will use these building blocks to make your first cream and to write your own formula in percentages and grams.

takeaways: A cream has a water phase, an oil phase with an emulsifying wax, and a cool-down phase.
Beeswax is not an emulsifier; use a named emulsifying wax at the supplier's rate.
Use distilled or deionised water, never tap or sachet water.
Preservatives usually go in during cool-down because heat can damage them.
Every formula must add up to 100 percent.

lessons.title: Equipment, sanitation and safe working for water-based products
objectives: List the equipment needed to make creams accurately
Clean and sanitise tools and containers correctly
Prepare 70 percent alcohol from a stronger bottle
Work safely with hot liquids and electricity

blocks.text: Water-based products are only as clean as the tools, jars and hands that touch them. This lesson sets up the routine you will repeat for every batch. Doing it the same way every time is what makes your creams safe and consistent.

blocks.name: gloves
blocks.caption: Clean gloves are a simple barrier between your hands and a product that customers will put on their skin.

blocks.text: Equipment you need

head: Item
Why it matters
rows: Preservatives at 0.5% of a 200 g batch are just 1 g; a kitchen scale is not accurate enough
Heat-resistant glass jugs or stainless steel bowls (two)
One for the water phase, one for the oil phase
Pot for a water bath, or a hotplate
You heat to about 75°C and add the preservative below its maximum temperature
Creates small, stable droplets; hand stirring alone often separates
pH meter or narrow-range pH strips
To check the cream is inside the preservative's working range
Jars, pump bottles or tubes with lids
Pumps and tubes keep fingers out of the product

blocks.text: Clean first, then sanitise
**Cleaning** removes dirt and grease. **Sanitising** kills most of the germs that remain. You need both, in that order, because dirt protects germs from the sanitiser.

items: Wash all tools, jugs and containers in hot water with dish soap. Rinse well.
Let them dry fully on a clean rack or wipe with a fresh paper towel, not a shared kitchen cloth.
Wipe your work surface with soap and water, then sanitise it.
Spray or wipe tools, jars, lids and blender head with 70% isopropyl alcohol and let it evaporate completely.
Wash hands, put on clean gloves and spray the gloves with 70% alcohol before you start.

blocks.text: Why 70 percent and not 99 percent? Making Skincare explains that 70% isopropyl alcohol is more effective than 100% because the water in it helps denature the proteins of microorganisms. Pharmacies in Nigeria commonly sell isopropyl alcohol; check the percentage on the label.

blocks.title: Worked example: diluting 99% alcohol to about 70%
blocks.context: For example, Bisi in Ibadan can only find 99% isopropyl alcohol and wants a 500 ml spray bottle of roughly 70% sanitiser.
steps: She works out how much 99% alcohol gives 70% of 500 ml: 500 × 70 ÷ 99 = about 354 ml.
She measures 354 ml of 99% isopropyl alcohol into a clean measuring jug.
She tops up with distilled water to the 500 ml mark and stirs gently.
She labels the bottle "Isopropyl alcohol approx. 70%, flammable, for cleaning tools only" with the date.
blocks.result: Bisi has about 500 ml of roughly 70% sanitiser for her tools and surfaces, mixed from the stronger stock she could find.

blocks.title: Before you heat anything
items: Tools washed and dried
Surfaces and tools sanitised
Hair covered, gloves on
Formula printed and weighed
Scale tared and accurate
Children and pets out
blocks.caption: Tick every item before turning on the heat; a missed step is hard to fix halfway through a batch.

blocks.text: Safety with heat, alcohol and electricity

blocks.title: Hot liquids and flammable alcohol
blocks.text: Isopropyl alcohol is highly flammable. Never spray it near a gas flame or a hot burner, and let it evaporate fully before you switch on heat. Melted wax and water at 75°C can cause serious burns: use oven gloves, keep handles turned inward, and keep children out of the kitchen. Never leave a pot on heat unattended.

items: Keep the stick blender cable and sockets away from the water bath. Unplug the blender before touching the blade.
Use a stable, flat surface. A tipping jug of hot oil is the most common accident.
If NEPA (grid) power goes off mid-batch, do not leave a gas cooker unattended while you sort out the generator.
If hot wax or oil touches skin, cool it under cool running water for 20 minutes and seek medical help for large or deep burns.

blocks.text: Storing ingredients

Keep oils, butters and the emulsifying wax in closed containers away from sun and heat; light and heat speed up rancidity. Keep the preservative tightly closed and note its opening date. Keep distilled water sealed and never pour unused water back into the bottle. Store everything off the floor, away from kitchen food and out of children's reach.
Choosing containers for creams

Every time a customer dips fingers into an open jar, she adds germs and sometimes water to the cream. A pump bottle, a squeeze tube or a jar used with a small spatula reduces this. For lotions, pumps are the usual choice. For thicker creams, jars are common, so include a spatula or print "use clean, dry fingers or a spatula" on the label. Buy containers new and sealed, wash and sanitise them anyway, and let them dry fully before filling, because water droplets left inside a jar are an easy place for mould to start.

blocks.title: Make one corner your production corner
blocks.text: If you share a kitchen, choose one shelf and one box for skincare tools only. Do not use them for food. This prevents cross-contamination in both directions and makes your hygiene routine faster.

takeaways: Use a 0.01 g scale, thermometer, stick blender and pH meter for creams.
Clean with soap and water first, then sanitise with 70% isopropyl alcohol.
Alcohol is flammable: let it dry before any heat is switched on.
Treat 75°C liquids with care and keep children away during production.

quiz.q: Funke mixes shea butter, water and beeswax, and after two days the jar has water at the bottom. What is the main reason?
options: She used too little shea butter
Beeswax is not an emulsifier, so the water and oil separated
She did not add essential oil
quiz.explain: Beeswax thickens but does not emulsify. A named emulsifying wax is needed to hold water and oil together.

quiz.q: Which of these products does NOT need a preservative?
options: A facial oil made only from jojoba and baobab oil
quiz.explain: A blend of oils contains no water, so germs cannot multiply in the same way. It still needs protection from rancidity.

quiz.q: A recipe lists: water 70%, glycerin 5%, oils 18%, e-wax 5%, preservative 1%. What should Ada notice?
options: It totals 99%, so something is missing or wrong
quiz.explain: A complete formula always adds up to 100 percent. Before using it, she should find the missing 1 percent.

quiz.q: Why do you add the preservative in the cool-down phase?
options: Many preservatives are damaged above a maximum temperature
quiz.explain: Data sheets give a maximum temperature; for example, Liquid Germall Plus tolerates heat up to 50°C.

quiz.q: Ngozi has only 99% isopropyl alcohol. What is the best thing to do for sanitising her tools?

Dilute it to about 70% with distilled water
Skip sanitising and wash tools only
quiz.explain: 70% isopropyl alcohol is more effective than 100% because the water helps denature microbial proteins.

quiz.q: Which water should go into a cream?
options: Borehole water that has been boiled
quiz.explain: Minerals and other content in tap, borehole or bottled water can shorten shelf life, so distilled or deionised water is used.

modules.title: Guided practice: your first cream, your batch formula and a facial oil
modules.overview: Make a basic emulsified cream with the heat, hold, blend and cool method, then learn to write any formula in percentages and convert it to grams for any batch size. Finish by blending a facial oil that resists rancidity.

lessons.title: Making a basic emulsified cream: heat, hold, blend and cool
objectives: Heat the water and oil phases to the right temperature
Combine and blend the phases into a stable emulsion
Add the cool-down phase at the correct temperature
Recognise a good emulsion and a failing one

blocks.text: This lesson walks you through the full method for an oil-in-water cream using an emulsifying wax. The method is the same whether you make 100 g to practise or 5 kg to sell. What changes with experience is your speed, not the steps.

blocks.name: thermometer
blocks.caption: Temperature control is the heart of emulsion making: hot enough to melt and combine, cool enough to protect the preservative.

blocks.text: Before you start

Sanitise your workspace as in Module 1. Print or write your formula with the gram weight of every ingredient. Weigh the water phase into one heat-resistant jug and the oil phase, including the emulsifying wax, into another. Weigh the preservative into a small clean cup and set it aside, covered.
The method step by step

items: **Weigh the water jug.** Write down the total weight of the jug plus the water phase. You will use this to replace water lost as steam.

**Heat both phases.** Stand both jugs in a water bath (a pot with a few centimetres of simmering water) or on a hotplate. Making Skincare advises heating the water phase to around 75°C and holding it at that temperature for 20 minutes. Heat the oil phase to roughly the same temperature until the wax is fully melted; the oil phase does not need the 20-minute hold.
**Top up the water.** After the hold, wipe the outside of the water jug dry, weigh it again and add back hot distilled water to reach the weight you wrote down.
**Combine.** With both phases at a similar temperature, pour the oil phase into the water phase. If one is much cooler, the wax can set into lumps.
**Blend.** Put the stick blender head fully under the surface, then blend in short bursts for about a minute. Keeping the head submerged stops air bubbles being whipped in.

**Blend, cool, blend.** Humblebee & Me recommends a blend-cool-blend cycle: blend about a minute, leave about ten minutes, blend again, and repeat as it thickens. Stir gently with a spatula between bursts.

**Cool-down phase.** When the cream has cooled to about 45°C (the point Making Skincare gives) and is below your preservative's maximum temperature, add the preservative and any other cool-down ingredients. Mix very well so it is spread through the whole batch.
**Fill and rest.** Fill sanitised containers, leave the lids slightly open until the cream reaches room temperature to avoid condensation, then close and label with the batch code.

blocks.title: From two jugs to one cream
items: Weigh both phases
Heat to about 75°C
Hold water phase 20 minutes
Combine and blend
Cool to about 45°C
Add preservative, fill
blocks.caption: Each stage depends on the one before; rushing the heating or the cooling is the most common cause of a failed batch.

blocks.text: Why heat and hold?

Emulsifying waxes must be fully melted to work. Heating both phases to a similar temperature lets the wax spread evenly before it begins to set. Holding the water phase at temperature for a while is a common practice taught by formulation schools to reduce the germs in the water before the product is preserved. It does not replace the preservative: it simply gives the preservative a cleaner start.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 200 g practice cream timeline
blocks.context: For example, Chioma in Owerri makes her first 200 g practice cream on a Saturday morning using a tested learning formula with Emulsifying Wax NF.
steps: 9:00 She sanitises the counter and tools and weighs both phases. Water jug plus water phase: 412.40 g.
9:15 Both jugs go into the water bath. At 9:35 the water phase reads 75°C; she starts a 20-minute timer and keeps it between 73 and 77°C.
9:55 She dries and reweighs the water jug: 405.10 g. She adds 7.30 g of hot distilled water to get back to 412.40 g.
10:00 Oil phase at 74°C, water at 75°C. She pours oil into water and blends for one minute.
10:10 to 10:40 Three more blend-cool-blend rounds. The mixture turns white and thick.
10:50 Thermometer reads 44°C. She adds 1.00 g preservative, stirs for two minutes and fills two 100 g jars.
blocks.result: Chioma's cream is smooth and white with no oil on top. Without the water top-up, her cream would have been about 7 g short of water and slightly thicker than the formula intended.

blocks.text: Reading your result

head: What you see
Likely cause
What to try next time
rows: Oil pooling on top within hours
Too little emulsifier for the oil amount, or phases not hot enough
Check the e-wax rate for your oil percentage; make sure the wax fully melted
Phases at very different temperatures, wax set early
Bring both to a similar temperature before combining
Blender head lifted out of the liquid
Keep the head submerged and tilt the jug slightly
Thin at first, thicker next day
Normal: creams keep thickening as they cool fully
Judge texture after 24 hours, not straight away

blocks.title: Handle hot jugs carefully
blocks.text: Jugs at 75°C are hot enough to burn. Lift them with oven gloves, pour slowly onto a stable surface, and keep the blender cable away from the water bath.

blocks.title: Practice batches are for you only
blocks.text: Use your first creams yourself, and record how they behave over weeks. Do not give or sell any cream until you have completed the stability checks and preservative steps in Module 3.

takeaways: Heat the water phase to about 75°C and hold for 20 minutes; heat the oil phase to the same temperature.
Weigh the water jug before and after heating and add back lost distilled water.
Blend with the head submerged, using blend-cool-blend rounds.
Add the preservative at about 45°C and below its maximum temperature.
Judge the final texture after 24 hours.

lessons.title: Writing a batch formula in percentages and converting it to grams
objectives: Write a cream formula in percentages that totals 100
Convert percentages to grams for any batch size
Add a loss allowance so every container is full
Calculate small amounts such as the preservative accurately

blocks.text: Professional formulators write every recipe as percentages, not cups or spoons. Percentages let you make 100 g today and 5 kg next month with exactly the same result. They also make it easy to check preservative and emulsifier levels against the supplier's recommended range.

blocks.name: scales
blocks.caption: Accurate weighing turns a percentage formula into a repeatable product.

blocks.text: The one formula you need

**Grams of an ingredient = batch size in grams × percentage ÷ 100.** Humblebee & Me gives the same method for preservatives: a 50 g batch with a 2.5% ingredient needs 50 × 2.5 ÷ 100 = 1.25 g. Always weigh, never measure skincare ingredients by volume, because oils, glycerin and water all have different weights for the same volume.
A learning formula for a body cream

The formula below is a simple learning formula in the same style as published beginner lotions. It uses one named emulsifying wax and one named broad-spectrum preservative at a rate inside its published range. If you use a different emulsifier or preservative, change those lines to match your supplier's data sheet and adjust the water so the total is still 100.

Check the logic: oils total 20%, and the e-wax is 6%. Humblebee & Me writes that she uses 5 to 10% e-wax when oils are about 25%, so 6% for 20% oils is a reasonable starting point. Liquid Germall Plus is listed by the same source at 0.1 to 0.5%, with a working pH range of 3 to 8.

blocks.title: Worked example: converting to a 250 g batch
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat in Ilorin wants to fill five 50 g jars with the learning formula above.
steps: Batch size: 5 jars × 50 g = 250 g.
Distilled water: 250 × 70.5 ÷ 100 = 176.25 g.
Shea butter: 250 × 8 ÷ 100 = 20.00 g. Sunflower oil: 250 × 12 ÷ 100 = 30.00 g.
Emulsifying Wax NF: 250 × 6 ÷ 100 = 15.00 g.
Preservative: 250 × 0.5 ÷ 100 = 1.25 g.
blocks.result: Rukayat weighs 250 g of ingredients with a 0.01 g scale and every line matches her percentage formula exactly.

blocks.text: Allow for losses

Some cream always stays on the jug, spatula and blender. If you make exactly 250 g you may only fill four and a half jars. A simple fix is to add an allowance, for example 5 to 10 percent, to the batch size before you convert. For five 50 g jars with a 6% allowance, make 250 × 1.06 = 265 g and convert every line from 265 g. The preservative becomes 265 × 0.5 ÷ 100 = 1.33 g (rounded).

blocks.title: From idea to grams
items: Formula in percent
Check total is 100
Choose batch size
Add loss allowance
Grams = size × % ÷ 100
Re-add and check
blocks.caption: Following the same six steps every time prevents the small arithmetic errors that ruin batches.

blocks.text: Rounding and small amounts

items: Round to two decimal places when using a 0.01 g scale.
Never round the preservative down to zero or up beyond the supplier's maximum. In a 100 g test batch, 0.5% is 0.50 g, which a kitchen scale cannot weigh.
When you change one ingredient, adjust the water (the largest ingredient) so the total stays at 100%.
Keep one master sheet per product: percentages at the top, gram columns for each batch size below.

blocks.title: Use a phone spreadsheet
blocks.text: In Google Sheets or Excel on your phone, put percentages in column B and the batch size in one cell, for example E1. In column C type =E1*B2/100 and copy it down. Change E1 and every gram weight updates. Add a total row with =SUM to catch mistakes.

blocks.title: Do not increase the preservative "to be safe"
blocks.text: Using more than the maximum on the data sheet can irritate skin and does not make the product safer. Using less can leave it under-protected. Stay inside the published range and confirm with testing.

Once your master sheet is set up, scaling is quick. Making 2 kg for a market day is simply a matter of changing the batch size cell, checking your largest jug and pot are big enough, and allowing more time for heating and cooling. Large batches cool more slowly, so the cool-down step will take longer.
Adjusting texture without breaking the formula

Once your first batch works, you may want a richer cream or a thinner lotion. Change one thing at a time. For a richer feel, raise the shea butter by 2% and lower the water by 2%. For a thinner lotion, lower the oils and add the same amount to the water. If you raise the total oils a lot, check that your e-wax is still inside the range for that oil level. Write each version as a new line on your master sheet, such as Version 1.1 and Version 1.2, so you always know which formula produced which result.

takeaways: Grams = batch size × percentage ÷ 100.
A formula must total 100%; adjust water when you change other lines.
Add a 5 to 10% loss allowance so every container is full.
Weigh everything on a 0.01 g scale and keep the preservative inside its published range.

activity.title: Build your master formula sheet
steps: Create a spreadsheet or notebook page with the learning formula in percentages.
Add gram columns for 100 g, 265 g and 1,000 g.
Fill in every gram weight using the formula and check each column totals correctly.
Change the oil from sunflower to sweet almond and confirm the total is unchanged.
Ask a friend to check one column of your arithmetic.
activity.evidence: A screenshot or photo of your master formula sheet with all three batch sizes.

lessons.title: Facial oils and serums: choosing oils, blending and preventing rancidity
objectives: Describe the difference between a facial oil and a water-based serum
Choose carrier oils for a facial oil blend
Weigh a 30 ml facial oil batch accurately
Protect oil blends from going rancid

blocks.text: Facial oils are one of the simplest and most rewarding products to make well. There is no water, no emulsifier and no preservative. Instead, quality depends on choosing good oils, keeping them fresh and packaging them so light and air do less damage.

blocks.name: droplet
blocks.caption: A facial oil is used a few drops at a time, so freshness and a good dropper bottle matter more than volume.

blocks.text: Facial oil or serum?

The word "serum" is used loosely in shops. Some serums are oil blends, often called oil serums. Others are water-based, made with aloe vera juice, hydrosols or water thickened into a gel. A water-based serum follows all the rules of a cream: it needs a broad-spectrum preservative, a stable pH and testing. In this lesson you make an oil serum, which is anhydrous.

blocks.title: Oil serum versus water-based serum
items: Oil serum (facial oil)
Water-based serum
blocks.caption: The two look similar in a bottle but need completely different care in production.

blocks.text: Choosing oils

head: Oil
Notes for a facial blend
rows: Technically a liquid wax, not a true oil, so it is very stable and slow to go rancid; light feel
An African seed oil; medium feel; a good local story for your brand
Southern African oil; light to medium feel
Light and popular for faces, but goes rancid quickly; use as a smaller part of the blend and keep cool
Very light and stable; often sold made from olives or sugar cane

blocks.text: The Institute of Personal Care Science, in its video below, shows how choosing lighter oils makes a face oil feel less greasy. A practical rule: build most of the blend from a stable, light base (such as jojoba or squalane) and add a smaller amount of a delicate oil such as rosehip.
Rancidity: the enemy of oils

Oils react with oxygen over time and go rancid. You notice a sharp, crayon-like or paint-like smell. Heat, light and air speed this up, and oils rich in delicate fatty acids, such as rosehip, change fastest. Rancid oils can irritate skin and customers will notice the smell.

items: Buy fresh oil in quantities you will use within a few months, and ask the supplier for the batch and best-before date.
Add an antioxidant such as vitamin E (tocopherol) at the rate your supplier recommends. It slows rancidity; it is not a preservative.
Fill amber or cobalt blue glass dropper bottles, filled close to the top to leave less air.
Store stock oils and finished bottles away from sunlight and heat, not on a hot shop shelf facing the window.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 30 ml facial oil batch
blocks.context: For example, Efe in Benin City wants to fill one 30 ml amber dropper bottle. Most plant oils weigh a little less than water, roughly 0.9 g per ml, so she plans 27 g of oil.
steps: Formula: jojoba 50%, baobab 30%, rosehip 19.5%, vitamin E 0.5%. Total 100%.
Rosehip: 27 × 19.5 ÷ 100 = 5.27 g (rounded). Vitamin E: 27 × 0.5 ÷ 100 = 0.14 g (rounded).
She weighs straight into a sanitised, dry glass beaker on a 0.01 g scale, stirs with a clean glass rod, and pours through a small funnel into the bottle.
She labels it with the batch code and date and records the supplier batch of each oil.
blocks.result: Efe has a full 30 ml bottle with a written formula she can repeat exactly. If she switches to a 15 ml bottle, she only changes the batch size to about 13.5 g.

blocks.title: Essential oils and faces
blocks.text: Facial skin is more sensitive than body skin, and some essential oils, especially citrus oils such as bergamot, can make skin react to sunlight. For your first facial oil, leave essential oils out entirely. A fragrance-free face oil is easier to sell to customers with sensitive skin.

blocks.title: Keep it dry
blocks.text: Water from a wet bathroom or wet fingers can get into a dropper bottle. Advise customers to use the dropper, close the bottle straight after use and keep it out of the shower area.
Hygiene still matters

No water does not mean no hygiene. Sanitise the beaker, glass rod, funnel and bottles with 70% alcohol and let them dry completely, because any drop of water or alcohol left inside ends up in the oil. Wear gloves, keep droppers in their sealed bags until filling, and never dip a used dropper back into your stock oil. Clean, dry equipment is what keeps an anhydrous product truly water-free.

Facial oils are usually pressed into slightly damp skin after cleansing, or a few drops mixed into a cream. Write simple directions such as "Warm 3 to 4 drops between fingertips and press onto clean skin, night or morning" on your label or card. In Module 4 you will cost this bottle and decide its price.

takeaways: Oil serums contain no water; water-based serums need a preservative like any cream.
Build blends on a stable, light base and add delicate oils in smaller amounts.
Vitamin E slows rancidity but is not a preservative.
Weigh facial oils by grams (about 0.9 g per ml) and use dark glass bottles.

activity.title: Blend and record a facial oil
steps: Choose three oils you can buy locally or online and write a percentage formula totalling 100%.
Convert it to grams for one 30 ml or 15 ml bottle.
Weigh, blend and bottle it using sanitised, dry equipment.
Smell and photograph it on day 1 and again after 4 weeks, noting any change.
Record supplier, batch and best-before date for each oil.
activity.evidence: Your formula sheet with grams, the labelled bottle photo and your 4-week smell note.

quiz.q: Grace heats her water phase to 75°C for 20 minutes and finds the jug is 6 g lighter. What should she do?
options: Add 6 g of hot distilled water back before combining
quiz.explain: Water lost as steam changes the formula. Weighing before and after and adding back distilled water keeps the percentages correct.

quiz.q: A formula has preservative at 0.5%. How much is needed for a 400 g batch?
Joy's cream has oil pooling on top a few hours after making. Which is the most likely cause?
options: Too little emulsifier for her oil amount, or the wax did not fully melt
quiz.explain: Oil separation usually means the emulsifier could not hold that much oil, or it never melted and spread properly.

quiz.q: Why should the stick blender head stay under the surface while blending?
options: To stop air being whipped in as bubbles
quiz.explain: Lifting the head whips in air, giving a foamy cream full of bubbles.

quiz.q: Efe's facial oil smells like old crayons after three months on a sunny shelf. What happened?
options: Germs grew because there was no preservative
The oils went rancid from light, heat and air
quiz.explain: A crayon or paint smell is rancidity. Light and heat speed it up; dark bottles and cool storage slow it down.

quiz.q: Rukayat wants five 50 g jars and adds a 6% loss allowance. What batch size should she calculate from?
quiz.explain: 250 × 1.06 = 265 g, so there is enough to fill every jar after losses in the jug and blender.

modules.title: Quality and safety: preservatives, pH, stability, labels and NAFDAC
modules.overview: Choose and use a broad-spectrum preservative correctly, measure and adjust pH, and run simple stability checks that show whether your cream stays safe and unchanged. Then write an accurate ingredient list and understand the NAFDAC basics for selling creams.

lessons.title: Using a broad-spectrum preservative correctly and checking pH
objectives: Explain why a cream needs a broad-spectrum preservative
Read a preservative's data sheet for usage rate, pH range and heat limit
Measure the pH of a cream with a calibrated meter or strips
Adjust pH safely in small steps

blocks.text: Your cream is mostly water. Bacteria, yeasts and moulds can grow in that water, often without any sign you can see or smell at first. A **broad-spectrum preservative** is one that is designed to control all three groups. Humblebee & Me puts the rule simply: if you are making something that contains water, you need a broad-spectrum preservative. This lesson is about using one properly, because a preservative only works when it is chosen, dosed and kept within its pH range correctly.

blocks.name: petri-dish
blocks.caption: Microbes grow quietly in water-based products, which is why preservative choice and pH are checked, not guessed.

blocks.text: What "broad-spectrum" means

Some ingredients only work against bacteria, others only against moulds. A broad-spectrum preservative, or a ready-made blend, covers bacteria, yeasts and moulds together. Humblebee & Me lists several widely used examples, including Liquid Germall Plus, Optiphen Plus, Phenonip, NeoDefend and a gluconolactone and sodium benzoate blend, and warns that each has different strengths and weaknesses, so you cannot simply swap one for another.
Read the technical data sheet
Buy your preservative from a supplier who gives a **technical data sheet (TDS)**. From it, copy four facts into your notebook:

items: **Usage rate:** for example, Liquid Germall Plus is used at 0.1 to 0.5% according to Humblebee & Me.
**pH range:** the pH at which it works. For Liquid Germall Plus the same source gives pH 3 to 8.
**Maximum temperature:** Liquid Germall Plus tolerates heat up to 50°C, so it goes into the cool-down phase.
**Restrictions:** any product types or skin areas it is not recommended for, and its INCI name for your label.

blocks.title: Not preservatives
blocks.text: Vitamin E, rosemary extract, grapefruit seed extract, honey, salt and essential oils do not replace a broad-spectrum preservative in a cream. If a seller calls one of these a "natural preservative" for lotions, ask for a data sheet and test results.
Why pH matters

pH measures how acidic or alkaline something is, on a scale where 7 is neutral, lower is acidic and higher is alkaline. Healthy skin is slightly acidic: a study by Lambers and colleagues in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science (2006) found natural skin surface pH is on average below 5. Many creams are made slightly acidic to suit skin, but the deciding rule for you is simpler: **the finished cream must sit inside your preservative's working pH range**, or the preservative may not protect it.
Measuring pH

items: Wait until the cream is at room temperature, usually the next day; pH readings change with temperature.
Calibrate a pH meter with buffer solutions (commonly pH 4 and pH 7) following its instructions. Strips are cheaper but less precise; choose narrow-range strips if you use them.
Put a small sample into a clean cup. Never dip the meter into the whole batch.
Record the reading on your batch sheet. Rinse the probe with distilled water and store it as the instructions say.

blocks.title: Adjusting pH in small steps
items: Measure a sample
Add a few drops
Mix thoroughly
Wait and re-measure
Record the result
blocks.caption: Go round the cycle slowly; adding a lot at once can push pH far past your target.

blocks.title: Worked example: bringing a cream into range
blocks.context: For example, Toyin in Abeokuta makes a 500 g cream with a preservative whose data sheet says it works best below pH 5.5. Her next-day reading is 6.4.
steps: She dissolves 5 g of citric acid in 5 g of distilled water to make a 50% solution in a small labelled bottle.
She adds 3 drops to the whole batch, stirs for two minutes and measures a fresh sample: 6.0.
She adds 3 more drops, stirs and measures again: 5.6.
She adds 2 drops, stirs and measures: 5.2, which is inside the preservative's range.
She writes on the batch sheet: "pH 6.4 adjusted to 5.2 with 8 drops of 50% citric acid solution".
blocks.result: Toyin's preservative can now work as designed, and next time she knows roughly how much acid a 500 g batch needs.

blocks.title: Handle acids carefully
blocks.text: Citric acid is a food-grade acid but can sting eyes and broken skin. Wear gloves, label the solution clearly and keep it away from children. Add acid in drops, never by pouring.
The limits of home checks

Correct dose and pH give your preservative its best chance, but they do not prove it works in your exact formula. The recognised proof is a **preservative efficacy test**, often called a challenge test, done by a laboratory: the lab adds known microbes to your product and checks that the preservative reduces them over several weeks. Before selling at scale, budget for laboratory testing; NAFDAC registration also requires a laboratory certificate of analysis, which you will meet in Lesson 3.3.

takeaways: Any product containing water needs a broad-spectrum preservative.
Copy the usage rate, pH range, heat limit and INCI name from the data sheet.
The finished cream must sit inside the preservative's working pH range.
Adjust pH with small amounts of citric acid solution and re-measure each time.
A laboratory challenge test is the recognised proof that a preservative works.

activity.title: Preservative and pH record
steps: Write the four data sheet facts for the preservative you plan to use.
Measure the pH of your practice cream the day after making it.
If it is outside the range, adjust in small steps and record each reading.
Calculate how many grams of preservative your 250 g batch needs and check it is inside the range.
activity.evidence: A photo of your preservative fact card and the pH readings written on your batch sheet.

lessons.title: Stability testing and batch records for creams and oils
objectives: Set up a simple home stability test at three temperatures
Recognise the signs that a cream or oil is failing
Keep a batch record that traces every jar back to its ingredients
Decide on a cautious shelf life and use-by period

blocks.text: A cream can look perfect on day one and separate, change smell or grow mould weeks later. **Stability testing** means storing samples under different conditions and checking them regularly so you find these problems before your customers do.

blocks.name: spiral-calendar-pad
blocks.caption: Stability testing runs on a calendar: the same checks, on fixed dates, for every new formula.

blocks.text: A simple three-temperature test

Making Skincare describes a three-month stability test with samples kept at room temperature, in a fridge at about 4°C, and in a warm place at 40 to 45°C, checked at 2, 4, 8, 12 and 24 weeks. Heat speeds up most kinds of failure, so the warm sample often shows problems first. In Nigeria, room temperature itself is often warm, which makes this test especially useful.

items: Fill at least three small, sanitised, identical jars from the same batch and label each with the batch code and where it will be stored.
Keep one at room temperature away from direct sun, one in the fridge, and one in a warm place checked with your thermometer. Keep a fourth sealed jar untouched as a reference.
On each check date, look, smell, feel and measure pH, and write results in your log.
Compare every sample with the reference jar and with your day-one photo.

blocks.title: Stability check dates
items: Day 1: photo and pH
Week 2 check
Week 4 check
Week 8 check
Week 12 check
Week 24 check
blocks.caption: Checking on fixed dates turns vague impressions into a record you can compare between versions.

blocks.text: What to look for

head: Check
Good sign
Warning sign
rows: Oil or water separating, spots, colour change
Within a small range of day one and inside preservative range

blocks.title: Any mould means stop
blocks.text: If any sample shows mould, fuzzy spots or a sour smell, do not use or sell anything from that batch. Review your hygiene, preservative dose and pH, and make a new test batch.
Batch records

A batch record is the story of one batch: what went in, how it was made and what came out. Give every batch a code, for example NC-2610-01 for Natural Cream, October 2026, batch 1. Print the code on every jar.

items: Date, batch code, product name and formula version.
Each ingredient with planned and actual weight, supplier and supplier batch number.
Temperatures and times for heating, holding and cool-down.
pH before and after any adjustment.
Number of containers filled and any problems.
Stability and customer feedback notes added later.

blocks.title: Worked example: two versions compared
blocks.context: For example, Uche in Aba tests two versions of her body cream, version 1.0 with 5% e-wax and version 1.1 with 6% e-wax, side by side for eight weeks.
steps: Week 2: both look fine at room temperature. In the warm sample, version 1.0 has a thin oily line on top.
Week 4: version 1.0 warm sample has clearly separated. Version 1.1 is unchanged in all three places.
Week 8: version 1.1 pH has moved from 5.3 to 5.4, still inside the preservative range; smell and texture unchanged.
She records version 1.0 as failed and continues testing version 1.1 to week 12 before any sale.
blocks.result: The warm sample revealed a weak emulsion in four weeks, saving Uche from selling a cream that would have separated in customers' bags.

blocks.text: Setting a cautious shelf life

Do not print a long expiry date you have not tested. If your samples have only been checked for 12 weeks, do not claim two years. A cautious approach is to set the shelf life no longer than the period your tests and any laboratory results support, and to add a "use within" period after opening, such as 6 months, shown with the open-jar symbol. Extend dates only when longer tests support it.
Facial oils need stability checks too

For a facial oil the main risk is rancidity, not germs. Keep one bottle at room temperature away from light and one in a warm place, and smell both against a fridge-stored reference every month. If the warm bottle starts to smell sharp or like crayons after two months, your blend may not last long on a hot shop shelf. You can then lower the share of the delicate oil, such as rosehip, raise the share of a stable one such as jojoba, or switch to smaller bottles that customers finish sooner.

Also test your packaging. Fill one pump bottle and one jar from the same batch and use them yourself daily for a month. Note whether the pump clogs, whether the jar lid seals, and whether the label smudges with oily fingers. Packaging faults cause as many customer complaints as formula faults.

blocks.title: Use your phone
blocks.text: Photograph each sample on each check date against the same white paper and lighting, and keep the photos in a folder named with the batch code. Side-by-side photos make small changes easy to see.

takeaways: Test samples at room temperature, in a fridge and in a warm place.
Check at fixed dates: 2, 4, 8, 12 and 24 weeks.
Separation, smell change, mould or big pH drift mean the batch fails.
Every jar carries a batch code linked to a full batch record.
Never print a shelf life longer than your tests support.

activity.title: Start a stability test
steps: Fill four small jars from your practice cream and label them Room, Fridge, Warm and Reference.
Create a log with columns for date, look, smell, feel and pH.
Record day-one results and photos.
Set phone reminders for weeks 2, 4, 8 and 12.
Write the batch record for this batch using the list above.
activity.evidence: Your batch record, your stability log with day-one entries and photos of the labelled jars.

lessons.title: Ingredient safety, honest ingredient lists and NAFDAC basics for creams
objectives: Write an ingredient list for a cream using INCI names in the right order
Identify ingredients that must never go into a cream
Flag allergens and sensitivities honestly on the label
Outline what NAFDAC requires before a cream is sold

blocks.text: A cream label has more to say than a butter label: more ingredients, a preservative, and often a use-by period after opening. Customers with sensitive skin read these lists closely. This lesson focuses on getting the ingredient list right for an emulsion and keeping dangerous ingredients out.

blocks.name: document-analysis
blocks.caption: An ingredient list is a document customers rely on, so every line must match what is really in the jar.

blocks.text: Writing the ingredient list

Use **INCI names**, the international standard names for cosmetic ingredients that suppliers print on their data sheets, and list ingredients in order of weight, largest first. A blend such as an emulsifying wax or a preservative is listed as its separate parts. Your supplier's data sheet gives these INCI names; if they cannot, find a supplier who can.

blocks.title: Worked example: the learning formula as an ingredient list
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat turns the Module 2 body cream (water 70.5%, sunflower oil 12%, shea 8%, Emulsifying Wax NF 6%, glycerin 3%, Liquid Germall Plus 0.5%) into a label.
steps: Water becomes Aqua (Water). Sunflower oil becomes Helianthus Annuus (Sunflower) Seed Oil. Shea becomes Butyrospermum Parkii (Shea) Butter.

Emulsifying Wax NF is listed by Humblebee & Me as Cetostearyl (Cetearyl) Alcohol and Polysorbate 60, so both names appear. She asks her supplier how the 6% splits between them to place each correctly.
Liquid Germall Plus is Propylene Glycol, Diazolidinyl Urea and Iodopropynyl Butylcarbamate; these small amounts go near the end.

Draft list: Aqua (Water), Helianthus Annuus (Sunflower) Seed Oil, Butyrospermum Parkii (Shea) Butter, Cetearyl Alcohol, Glycerin, Polysorbate 60, Propylene Glycol, Diazolidinyl Urea, Iodopropynyl Butylcarbamate.
blocks.result: Rukayat's list is complete and honest, and she will confirm the order of the emulsifier parts with her supplier before printing.

blocks.title: Cream label checklist
items: INCI ingredients, largest first
Net weight and batch code
Manufacture date and use-by
Directions and external use only
Allergen and patch test warnings
Maker's name and address
blocks.caption: Run this checklist against every new label before you print.

blocks.text: Ingredients that must never go into your cream

Creams are the product most often used to hide harmful "toning" or "lightening" ingredients. Never add hydroquinone, mercury compounds, steroid creams, antibiotic or antifungal creams, crushed tablets or any medicine. These can cause serious harm, and adding them turns your product into an unregistered medicine. If a customer asks you to "add something strong", say no and explain that you make cosmetic moisturisers only.
Allergens and sensitivities

items: **Nut-derived oils** such as sweet almond or macadamia: state them clearly, for example "contains almond oil".
**Essential oils and fragrance:** common causes of skin reactions; keep them low or leave them out, especially in face products.

**Preservatives:** some customers avoid particular preservatives. Diazolidinyl urea, for example, is known as a formaldehyde-releasing preservative, so people with that sensitivity will check for it. Listing every preservative by name lets them choose.
**Patch test advice:** print "Patch test before first use. Stop use if irritation occurs."

blocks.text: Directions also protect customers. For a body lotion, for example: "Smooth onto clean skin as needed. For external use only. Avoid the eyes. Keep out of reach of children. Store below 30°C away from direct sunlight. Use within 6 months of opening." Only print a storage temperature or use-by period that your own stability tests support, and adjust the wording to your product.

Ingredient safety also includes the raw materials themselves. Buy from suppliers who give data sheets and batch numbers, store each material in its original labelled container, and never transfer a preservative or acid into an unmarked food bottle where someone could mistake it for something else. If a raw material arrives without a label, smells wrong or has passed its best-before date, do not use it.
Honest words for creams

Describe what a cosmetic cream really does: moisturises, softens, helps skin feel comfortable. Avoid claims to treat eczema, acne, stretch marks, dark spots or any condition. Be careful with "natural" and "preservative-free". A cream with Liquid Germall Plus is not preservative-free, and saying so would be false and unsafe. You can honestly write "made with shea butter and sunflower oil, preserved for your safety".
NAFDAC basics

In Nigeria, cosmetics are regulated by NAFDAC. Its Guidelines for the Registration of Cosmetics Made in Nigeria require, among other documents, business registration (a CAC business name is accepted for micro and small enterprises), trademark evidence for the brand name, an inspection of the premises, label artwork that complies with the Cosmetics Labelling Regulations, and a laboratory certificate of analysis. NAFDAC also runs services for micro, small and medium enterprises. Read the current guideline on the NAFDAC website or visit the nearest NAFDAC office before you apply, as requirements and fees are updated.

blocks.title: Your records are your evidence
blocks.text: The batch records, stability logs, data sheets and pH readings you have been keeping are exactly the kind of evidence an inspector expects to see. Keep them in one folder per product from your first batch.

takeaways: List ingredients by INCI name, largest first, including every part of the e-wax and preservative.
Never add hydroquinone, mercury, steroids, antibiotics or any medicine.
Name nut oils, fragrance and preservatives so sensitive customers can choose.
A preserved cream is not preservative-free; say what is true.
NAFDAC registration needs business, trademark, inspection, label and lab documents.

activity.title: Draft a compliant cream label
steps: Write the INCI ingredient list for your own cream formula in order of weight.
Ask your supplier for any INCI names or splits you do not know.
Add net weight, batch code, dates, directions, warnings and your name and address.
Check the draft against the six-point checklist and remove any medical or false claims.
Download the NAFDAC cosmetics registration guideline and list the documents you already have.
activity.evidence: Your draft label (handwritten or Canva) and your NAFDAC document checklist.

quiz.q: Bola's preservative data sheet says it works from pH 3 to 8. Her cream measures pH 8.6. What should she do?
options: Sell it, pH does not matter
Lower the pH in small steps until it is inside the range, then re-measure
quiz.explain: A preservative may not protect the product outside its working pH range. Adjust in small steps and re-measure.

quiz.q: Which of these is a broad-spectrum preservative suitable for a lotion?
options: Liquid Germall Plus used at its stated rate
quiz.explain: Liquid Germall Plus is a broad-spectrum preservative. The others are antioxidants or fragrance and do not reliably control bacteria, yeast and mould.

quiz.q: In a stability test, Kemi's warm sample separates at week 4 but the room temperature sample looks fine. What does this most likely mean?
options: The warm sample was just unlucky
The emulsion is weak and will probably fail later at room temperature too
She should only sell in cool months
quiz.explain: Heat speeds up failure. A warm sample that separates warns of a weak emulsion that may separate in customers' homes.

quiz.q: A customer asks Amina to label her preserved lotion "preservative-free" because it sounds natural. What should Amina do?
options: Refuse: it contains a preservative, so the claim is false
quiz.explain: The claim would be false. Removing the preservative would also make the lotion unsafe.

quiz.q: How should the ingredients be ordered on a cream label?
options: By weight, largest first, using INCI names
quiz.explain: Ingredient lists use INCI names in descending order of weight.

quiz.q: Uche has only tested her cream for 12 weeks. What shelf life should she print?
options: No longer than her tests and lab results support
quiz.explain: A cautious shelf life is no longer than the evidence supports; extend it only after longer tests.

modules.title: Costing, selling and your product development project
modules.overview: Work out the true cost of a jar of cream and a bottle of facial oil, including testing and labour, and set a price that leaves a profit. Then present your products honestly online and in person, and complete your documented product development project with a 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Costing a jar of cream and a bottle of facial oil
objectives: Calculate the cost per gram of each ingredient
Cost a full batch including packaging, energy, labour and testing
Work out cost per container
Set a price using a target profit margin

blocks.text: Creams look cheap to make because most of the jar is water. But emulsifying wax, preservative, better packaging, labels and laboratory tests add up quickly. Many new makers price by guessing what others charge and only discover later that they lose money on every jar. This lesson uses your batch formula from Module 2 to find the real cost.

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.alt: A person using a large calculator
blocks.caption: Costing is simple arithmetic done carefully, once per product, and updated when prices change.

blocks.title: About the prices in this lesson
blocks.text: All naira prices here are approximate examples for practice only. Prices vary by city, supplier and month. Use the prices on your own receipts.
Step 1: cost per gram

For each ingredient, divide what you paid by the grams you received. If 500 g of emulsifying wax cost ₦8,000, the cost per gram is 8,000 ÷ 500 = ₦16 per gram. For liquids sold by volume, weigh a full container on your scale once, or use roughly 0.9 g per ml for most plant oils. Then multiply each ingredient's cost per gram by the grams in your batch.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing five 50 g jars of body cream
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat costs the 265 g batch from Module 2 (five 50 g jars plus a loss allowance), using approximate prices from her receipts.
steps: Distilled water 186.82 g at about ₦0.75/g = ₦140. Glycerin 7.95 g at ₦6/g = ₦48.
Shea butter 21.20 g at ₦5/g = ₦106. Sunflower oil 31.80 g at about ₦4.89/g = ₦156.
Emulsifying Wax NF 15.90 g at ₦16/g = ₦254. Preservative 1.32 g at ₦100/g = ₦132. Ingredients total: ₦836.
Packaging: 5 jars with lids at ₦400 = ₦2,000. Labels: 5 at ₦100 = ₦500.
Gas or electricity ₦300. Gloves and alcohol ₦300. Her labour: 2 hours at ₦1,500 per hour = ₦3,000.
Testing set-aside: ₦150 per jar towards laboratory tests = ₦750.
blocks.result: The ingredients are only about ₦170 per jar; the real cost is about ₦1,540 once packaging, labour and testing are counted. Pricing at ₦1,000 because "it is mostly water" would lose money.

blocks.text: Step 2: price with a target margin

Profit **margin** is the share of the selling price that is profit. To price for a margin, use: **price = cost ÷ (1 − margin)**. For a 40% margin on a ₦1,540 jar: 1,540 ÷ 0.6 = ₦2,567, which Rukayat rounds to ₦2,600. Then she checks what similar 50 g creams sell for in her area. If her price is far higher, she looks for savings, such as buying jars in bulk, before cutting her margin.

blocks.title: From receipts to selling price
items: Cost per gram
Ingredient cost per batch
Add packaging and energy
Add labour and testing
Divide by containers
Apply target margin
blocks.caption: Leaving out any stage, especially labour and testing, makes a product look more profitable than it is.

blocks.text: Costing the facial oil

Facial oils are the opposite of creams: no water, so the oils are the biggest cost. Using Efe's 27 g blend from Module 2 with approximate prices: jojoba 13.50 g at ₦90/g = ₦1,215; baobab 8.10 g at ₦60/g = ₦486; rosehip 5.27 g at ₦80/g = ₦421; vitamin E 0.14 g = ₦22. Oils total about ₦2,145. Add an amber dropper bottle ₦700, label ₦100, sanitiser ₦50, half an hour of labour ₦750 and a testing set-aside of ₦150, and the bottle costs about ₦3,895. At a 40% margin the price is 3,895 ÷ 0.6 = about ₦6,500.
Ways to lower cost without lowering safety

items: Buy jars, bottles and emulsifying wax in larger quantities once your formula has passed stability tests.
Make larger batches: labour and energy per jar fall as batch size grows.
Group oil purchases with other makers in your WODDI network, if you trust the supplier's batch records.
Never save money by cutting the preservative, skipping pH checks or using tap water.

blocks.text: Do not forget failed batches

While you are learning, some batches will separate or fail stability tests. Those costs are real. A simple way to account for them is to add a small waste allowance to your costing, for example assuming that one batch in ten is lost, which adds about 10% to your cost per jar. As your method improves and fewer batches fail, you can reduce the allowance. Counting waste honestly stops you from feeling profitable on paper while your purse tells a different story.

blocks.title: Update costs every quarter
blocks.text: Prices of imported ingredients such as emulsifying wax and preservatives change with the exchange rate. Put your costing in the same spreadsheet as your formula and update the price column every three months, or whenever you restock.

takeaways: Cost per gram = price paid ÷ grams received.
Include packaging, energy, labour and a testing set-aside, not just ingredients.
Price = cost ÷ (1 − margin).
Creams are packaging and labour heavy; facial oils are ingredient heavy.
Never cut safety steps to lower cost.

activity.title: Cost your own products
steps: Collect receipts or current prices for every ingredient and package you use.
Calculate cost per gram for each ingredient.
Cost one batch of your cream and one bottle of facial oil, including labour and testing.
Set a price at a 40% margin and compare it with three similar products in your area.
Write one action you could take to lower cost safely.

lessons.title: Presenting and selling creams and facial oils honestly
objectives: Choose packaging that protects water-based products
Write a clear, honest product description for WhatsApp or a market stall
Answer common customer questions about creams accurately
Offer samples hygienically

blocks.text: Selling creams and facial oils is not only about attractive photos. Customers want to know how a product feels, how to use it, how long it lasts and whether it suits their skin. Clear, honest answers build the repeat customers that keep a small skincare business alive.

blocks.name: mobile-marketing
blocks.alt: A person promoting products on a mobile phone
blocks.caption: Most small skincare sales in Nigeria start with a phone: a clear catalogue entry and honest replies on WhatsApp.

blocks.text: Packaging that protects the product

blocks.title: Jar or pump for a cream?
items: Open jar
Pump bottle or tube
blocks.caption: For water-based products, packaging that keeps fingers out reduces contamination during use.

blocks.text: For facial oils, use amber or blue glass dropper bottles to cut light, and fill close to the top. Whatever you choose, test it during your stability checks so that pumps do not clog and labels do not smudge.
Packaging also carries your label, so choose containers with enough flat space for the full ingredient list, directions, warnings and batch code in a readable size.
Writing a product description
A good description answers five questions: what it is, how it feels, how to use it, what is in it, and how to store it. Keep it short enough to read on a phone screen.

blocks.title: Worked example: a WhatsApp Business catalogue entry
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat adds her body cream to her WhatsApp Business catalogue at the price she calculated in Lesson 4.1.
steps: Name and size: "Shea and Sunflower Daily Body Cream, 50 g".
Price: ₦2,600. Payment by bank transfer to her Moniepoint business account; she sends the account name in chat so customers can confirm it.

Description: "A light, non-greasy cream made with shea butter and sunflower oil. Smooth onto clean skin after bathing. Preserved for your safety. Use within 6 months of opening. Patch test before first use."
Photos: the jar against a plain background, the label with the full ingredient list readable, and a swatch on the back of her hand.
She adds a short line: "For dry skin comfort. Not a treatment for any skin condition."
blocks.result: Customers can see the price, texture, ingredients and directions before they ask, so Rukayat spends less time answering the same questions and her claims stay honest.

blocks.text: Answering common questions

head: Customer asks
Honest answer
rows: Will it lighten or tone my skin?
No. It is a moisturiser. It keeps skin soft and comfortable.
Is it all natural? Why is there a preservative?
The oils and butter are plant-based. Because it contains water, it needs a preservative to stop germs growing, which keeps you safe.
Can I use it on my baby?
I have not formulated or tested this for babies, so I cannot recommend it for them.
Use within 6 months of opening, before the date on the jar. Keep it out of direct sun.
Can I use the face oil with my cream?
Yes, many people press a few drops on after cream at night. Patch test first.

blocks.text: Samples, done safely

Samples help customers try a cream before buying a full jar. Fill small sanitised sample pots from a preserved, stability-tested batch, label each with the product name, batch code and "patch test before use", and never let customers dip fingers into a display tester jar. For market stalls, use a pump tester or a clean disposable spatula for each person.

blocks.title: Do not decant into unlabelled containers
blocks.text: Selling cream scooped into unlabelled nylon or reused containers removes the batch code, ingredients and directions, and exposes the product to germs. Sell only in sealed, labelled containers.
Building repeat sales

items: Ask every buyer, a week later, how the texture and smell suit them, and note it in your batch record.
Offer a facial oil as an add-on to cream customers who ask about face care.
Keep a simple customer list in a notebook or spreadsheet: name, product, date and feedback, with their permission to message them.
If a customer reports irritation, ask them to stop use, record the batch code and review that batch's records.

blocks.text: Taking orders and payment safely

Confirm each order in writing on WhatsApp: product, size, quantity, price, delivery fee and delivery date. Ask customers to pay by bank transfer and check the money has actually arrived in your Moniepoint, Opay or bank app before you hand over goods; screenshots of payment can be faked. When sending by dispatch rider, wrap pump bottles so the pump cannot be pressed in transit and tape jar lids. Ask customers to keep creams out of hot cars and direct sun, because heat shortens the life of any emulsion, however well it was made.

blocks.title: Show your process
blocks.text: Short videos of you sanitising, weighing and checking pH show customers that you take safety seriously. You do not need to reveal your exact formula to show your care.

takeaways: Pumps and tubes keep fingers out of water-based products; dropper bottles suit oils.
Describe what it is, how it feels, how to use it, what is in it and how to store it.
Answer questions about lightening, babies and preservatives honestly.
Give samples only from preserved, tested batches in labelled pots.

activity.title: Create your product listing
steps: Photograph your cream and facial oil with the labels readable.
Write a description for each covering the five questions.
Add them to WhatsApp Business catalogue or a printed price card.
Write honest answers to five questions customers are likely to ask you.
Ask two people to read the listing and tell you what is unclear.

lessons.title: Your product development project and 90-day plan
objectives: Assemble a complete product file for one cream or lotion
Present safety and stability evidence clearly
Reflect honestly on what worked and what to change
Write a 90-day plan with dated, measurable steps

blocks.text: Your project brings everything together. You will present one emulsified cream or lotion as a finished product, with the evidence that it was made cleanly, correctly preserved and tested. If you also made a facial oil, include it as a second product. The goal is a product file you could show to a buyer, a trainer or, later, a NAFDAC inspector.

blocks.name: certificate
blocks.caption: Your certificate reflects a real, documented product, not just reading.

blocks.text: What goes into your product file

items: **Formula sheet:** percentages totalling 100, gram columns for at least two batch sizes, and the version number.
**Data sheets:** for your emulsifying wax and preservative, with usage rate, pH range and heat limit highlighted.
**Batch record:** for your final batch, including temperatures, times, actual weights and pH readings.
**Stability log:** room, fridge and warm samples with photos, ideally to at least 8 weeks, and your conclusion.
**Personal use and feedback:** your own use notes and, where possible, feedback from at least one other adult after patch testing.
**Label and listing:** INCI ingredient list, warnings, directions and your catalogue description.
**Costing sheet:** cost per jar and price at your chosen margin.

blocks.title: A 90-day plan after the course
items: Days 1-14: finish stability checks
Days 15-30: first small sales
Days 31-60: feedback and version update
Days 61-75: price lab testing
Days 76-90: plan NAFDAC steps
blocks.caption: Each stage depends on evidence from the stage before, so sales grow only as fast as your testing allows.

blocks.text: Honest reflection

Write a short reflection of half a page. What went wrong in your first batches and how did you fix it? Did your stability test reveal anything? What feedback surprised you? Which numbers in your costing worried you? Honest reflection is more valuable than a perfect-looking file, because it shows you can find and fix problems on your own.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 90-day plan with numbers
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma in Onitsha has a body lotion that has passed 8 weeks of stability checks and a facial oil that has passed 12 weeks.
steps: Days 1 to 14: continue the lotion stability test to week 12; order 50 pump bottles once it passes.
Days 15 to 30: sell the facial oil to 10 existing butter customers at ₦6,500 and give 5 labelled lotion samples to adults who agree to give feedback.
Days 31 to 60: review feedback; if 3 or more say the lotion is too thin, make version 1.1 with 2% more shea and 2% less water and start a new stability test.
Days 61 to 75: ask two laboratories for quotes for a certificate of analysis and a preservative challenge test, and add the cost to her pricing.
Days 76 to 90: register her business name with CAC if not done, and list the documents still needed for NAFDAC registration.
blocks.result: Ifeoma has a plan where every step has a date and a number, and where selling the lotion widely waits for the testing that makes it safe.

blocks.text: Check before you submit

items: Open your formula sheet and confirm the percentages total 100 and the preservative is inside its published range.
Confirm your final batch pH is inside the preservative's working range and recorded.
Look at your stability photos: is there any separation, mould or smell change? If yes, explain what you will change.
Read your label aloud and remove any word that claims to treat, cure, lighten or heal.
Check your costing includes packaging, labour and a testing set-aside.

blocks.title: A product with unresolved problems is not ready
blocks.text: If your cream separated, grew mould or drifted out of the preservative's pH range, submit it with an honest explanation and a corrected plan rather than claiming it is ready to sell. Your certificate is stronger for it.

Over the next months, grow slowly: master one cream and one facial oil before adding more products. Each new product means a new formula, new stability tests and new label checks. A small range made consistently and honestly earns more trust, and more repeat customers, than a large range made in a hurry.
Presenting your project

Arrange your file in the same order every time: formula, data sheets, batch record, stability log, feedback, label and costing, then reflection and plan. Put a one-page summary at the front with the product name, version, batch code, final pH, how many weeks of stability testing it has passed, cost per container and price. A reviewer, buyer or inspector should be able to understand your product from that page in two minutes and find the detail behind every number in the pages that follow. Photograph each page clearly so you can share the file by WhatsApp or email if asked.

blocks.title: Keep learning
blocks.text: Formulation teaching sites such as Humblebee & Me and Making Skincare publish free articles on emulsifiers, preservatives and testing. Read the data sheet before every new ingredient, and change only one thing at a time.

takeaways: Your product file holds formula, data sheets, batch record, stability log, feedback, label and costing.
Honest reflection on problems is part of the evidence.
A 90-day plan needs dates and numbers, with sales paced by testing.
Master one cream and one oil before expanding.
